analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "In 1956, on a charge by the Labor Board, that the company and the certified bargaining agent had violated the rights of certain employees. The principal basis of the charge being that the company had lent illegal assistance to the union, and in that they deducted dues of the employees before they'd been with the company 30 days in violation of the statute. The complaint issued was served, and on January 1, 4, and 5, 1956, at the request of an attorney for the General Council, the regional director at Los Angeles issued subpoenas ad testificandum and dues esticum directed to the petitioners, under the seal of the board and under the facsimile signature of Aide Murdoch, a member of the board. On June 11, petitioners addressed petitions to revoke to the National Labor Relations Board, and in accordance with board rules, filed them with the regional director. We asserted that the board could not delegate its power to issue subpoenas to the regional director, and that an attorney for the General Council is not a party to an unfair labor practice proceedings, and hence he is not entitled to the issuance of subpoenas. As to the subpoenas dues esticum, petitioners Lewis and Schmidt also objected to the relevancy of the records and documents required to be produced. On that same day, the regional director referred the petitions to revoke to the trial examiner who denied the petitions. Petitioners refused to obey the subpoenas. The board, by its general council, on June 29, 1956, filed with the district court an application for an order requiring petitioners to obey the subpoenas. Petitioners resisted enforcement of the subpoenas on three grounds, that the regional director did not have authority to issue the subpoenas, that the trial examiner did not have authority to rule on the petition to revoke subpoenas, and that an attorney for the general council is not entitled to the issuance of subpoenas upon his application, since he is not a party to the proceedings. The objection to the relevancy of the documents was not renewed in the district court. On July 30, the district court issued its order quashing the subpoenas on the authority of NLRB v. Pesanti, 119 Fed Sub 444. I participated in the Pesanti case. It was our office that handled the case. And Judge Hall held in the Pesanti case that subpoenas issued under the facsimile signature of a board member are valid under the act, but that the statute provides that the board itself must pass upon the petition to revoke subpoenas, and he held further that an attorney for the general council is not a party to a board proceeding. Did that go to the court of appeals? No, Your Honor. The board did not take that case up, primarily, I believe, because the facts were not favorable to the board's position in that case. It was rather an extreme case, one where the subpoena was directed to 29 companies, directing the production of records, which the court notes would have required, in many cases, a small truck to bring before the board. The subpoenas compelled parties to travel bars 300 and 400 miles to Los Angeles to bring this evidence before a board agent who, at his leisure, could pursue the documents produced. Did the board offer to go to the offices themselves and make the documents in that case? Your Honor, it's my understanding that they did not participate in the case, and I do not recall any such offer. There was no appeal taken from the Pesanti case, but when this case came along, as a matter of principle, I objected to the procedure, which Judge Hall had found to be unlawful in the Pesanti case. I also objected to the relevancy of the documents. Judge Thurman Clark, in this case, on the authority of the Pesanti case, quashed the subpoenas. The board took an appeal to the District Court of Appeals, and the Court of Appeals reversed the order of the District Court. Frankly, I felt quite good inside when, during the opening argument by the board, Judge Barnes leaned over and asked consul, if stated to the consul, that the statute seemed to be rather clear on its face, and wasn't the board asking the court to engage in judicial legislation. But between that time and the time that Judge Barnes wrote the opinion, he apparently changed his views. I still believe that the Ninth Circuit has engaged in judicial legislation. The Ninth Circuit dealt only briefly with the question of the power to delegate authority to issue subpoenas, and they cited the Barnes case. And I want to state right here and now, for the benefit of the court, that although I raised that as one of my three questions, that on further study, I am convinced that there is no question of delegation insofar as the issuance of subpoenas is concerned. When I first got into this case, I felt the logic of my position on the power to rule on petitions to revoke subpoenas required my taking the same position insofar as the issuance of subpoenas is concerned. I also was of the view that the issuance question was the same in this case as it was in Cudahy and the Mohawk case, and I am satisfied that it is not. In the Cudahy and the Mohawk case, there was a certain element of discretion. Like Judge Barnes, you change your mind. Yes, Your Honor. In the Cudahy and the Mohawk case, there was a certain element of discretion in connection with the issuance of subpoenas. That is, the board could or could not, in its discretion, issue the subpoena. Under the National Labor Relations Act, Section 11, there is no discretion at the issuance stage. The issuance is now automatic. The board member signs. It's true he signs a facsimile, a rubber-stamped signature, but the subpoena is in the name of the board, and it is signed by one of the board members. The issuance itself is purely a ministerial act. I believe that Congress had in mind the federal court practice where clerks of the court issue subpoenas in blank, and if there's a contest, they're returnable for one of the judges. So that I am, as far as I'm concerned, conceding that there is no question of delegation here that it's purely a ministerial act because under the statute, the issuance of the subpoena is automatic, and I can see no useful purpose to be served by a requirement that the board itself or a member of the board actually issues the subpoena. Yes, Justice Whitaker, I'm speaking only of the issuance. Now, the signing, I think, is required by the act, but the ministerial act... Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
